CVE-2026-114938: OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Vulnerable To Pre-Authentication RCE (Java4Shell)
zscaler.com · 19 Nov 2026 02:39 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSapache-kafkaatlassian-confluenceatlassian-jiraavx-512-vbmibase64-intrinsicscve-2026-114938elasticsearchjava4shelljenkinsjfrog-artifactorykeycloakopenjdkoracle-graalvmoracle-java-sepingfederate
95
In plain words

The article describes Java4Shell, a serious flaw in some versions of Java that can let an outsider take control of a server by sending specially malformed text data. It can affect organizations using newer OpenJDK-based Java on certain Intel and AMD computers, including widely used services such as Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory, and PingFederate. Because this kind of text conversion is common in web logins, tokens, uploads, and other online communications, the flaw could expose many business applications before a user signs in. Organizations are urged to install updated Java versions quickly or temporarily turn off the affected speed-optimization feature.

Summary
CVE-2026-114938 (“Java4Shell”) is a critical OpenJDK Base64 intrinsic flaw that can enable pre-authentication RCE on AVX-512 VBMI-capable x86-64 systems when applications decode attacker-controlled malformed Base64 input. Patch affected JDKs immediately and, if patching is delayed, restart JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the vulnerable path.

CVE-2026-114938, known as Java4Shell, is a critical heap memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder that was publicly disclosed on November 17, 2026. The flaw affects certain x86-64 systems and can be reached when applications send attacker-controlled data to the affected decoder. Calif.io demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in default configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, while other products were shown vulnerable after authentication.

The vulnerable routine is produced by the HotSpot C2 compiler on processors supporting avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2, including newer Intel Xeon and AMD EPYC and Ryzen systems. Malformed Base64 input can trigger an arithmetic underflow that leads to a 62-byte out-of-bounds heap write; ARM64 systems and older x86-64 processors without AVX-512 VBMI are not affected. Organizations are advised to update to patched JDK builds and restart JVMs, or temporarily start affected JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the vulnerable optimized code path.

  • The issue is limited to a specific high-performance decoder path on x86-64 CPUs with four AVX-512-related capabilities, so affected organizations can assess exposure by checking for avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2 in Linux /proc/cpuinfo.
  • A temporary mitigation can disable the vulnerable Base64 optimization with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, but the alternative -XX:UseAVX=2 workaround must not be used on ARM64 systems because those JVMs will fail to start.
  • Reverse-proxy request buffering can disrupt exploitation methods that rely on several partially sent HTTP requests arriving at coordinated times, but it does not fully protect against single-request exploit chains or WebSocket tunnels.
  • The article describes a client-side TLS scenario in which a Java client connecting to a malicious server may be affected, extending the risk beyond publicly exposed Java servers.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-114938, also called Java4Shell, is a critical OpenJDK Base64 decoder flaw disclosed on November 17, 2026 that can cause a 62-byte heap out-of-bounds write on certain x86-64 processors.
  • 02The vulnerable code path requires x86-64 CPUs with avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2 support, while ARM64 processors and older x86-64 CPUs without AVX-512 VBMI are not affected.
  • 03Researchers demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in default configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate.
  • 04Organizations should upgrade to patched JDK builds and restart JVM processes and containers; where upgrades are delayed, they can use -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the affected optimized Base64 code path.
  • 05The article identifies indicators including Base64 warm-up request floods, partial HTTP requests used for heap grooming, malformed Base64 padding tails, spikes in IllegalArgumentException errors, and HotSpot crash logs.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a critical coordinated disclosure and patch advisory for a flaw that can enable pre-authentication remote code execution in widely deployed Java applications. Security professionals running affected OpenJDK builds on AVX-512-capable x86-64 systems should urgently identify exposure, patch, restart JVMs, or apply the documented temporary workaround.

    NGINX ( HTTP/2 ) – Critical Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-123007)
    netspi.com · 19 Nov 2026 00:29 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGScisa-kevcve-2026-113425cve-2026-121810cve-2026-123007cve-2026-123633cve-2026-123634f5http2-flow-controlinteger-underflownginxnginx-plusnvd
    In plain words

    F5 disclosed a serious flaw in nginx, widely used software that helps run websites and direct visitor traffic, when its newer HTTP/2 web connection feature is enabled. An unauthenticated person on the internet could potentially use it to view or alter the server’s memory, crash services, or take control of the software. It affects certain nginx and NGINX Plus versions, including systems embedded in containers and third-party appliances, so one exposed server could put multiple websites or backend services at risk. Organizations should install the fixed updates promptly or turn off HTTP/2 until they can patch.

    Summary
    F5 disclosed CVE-2026-123007, a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in nginx HTTP/2 that affects vulnerable nginx and NGINX Plus releases when HTTP/2 is enabled. Organizations should immediately upgrade to fixed releases or disable HTTP/2 until patching is complete.

    F5 disclosed CVE-2026-123007, a critical vulnerability in nginx’s HTTP/2 implementation, rated 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. The flaw can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to read and overwrite memory in an nginx worker process and potentially achieve remote code execution. It affects nginx Open Source versions 1.9.5 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8, as well as several NGINX Plus releases, when HTTP/2 is enabled.

    The underlying issue is an integer underflow in HTTP/2 flow-control accounting that can cause out-of-bounds memory reads and writes after queued data frames are cleaned up. The article states that researchers confirmed working unauthenticated remote code execution against affected builds, although no exploitation in the wild had been reported as of November 18, 2026. F5 fixed the flaw in nginx Open Source 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 and in NGINX Plus 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1; organizations unable to patch immediately can disable HTTP/2, but must also address other vulnerabilities included in the same release.

    • A reported nginx version alone may not determine exposure because Linux distribution packages can include the fix without changing the displayed nginx version, so organizations should compare their full package version with their distribution’s security advisory.
    • A configuration reload does not replace the vulnerable nginx executable; nginx must be restarted or undergo a supported live binary upgrade, and existing HTTP/2 connections can remain on old worker processes.
    • Although researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution, the article notes that a code-execution exploit may require substantial HTTP/2 traffic over one connection and may be less reliable on slower networks or through proxied HTTP/2 connections.
    • The same updates address several other serious flaws in HTTP/2, HTTP/3, DNS resolution, and mail proxy functionality, so disabling HTTP/2 alone does not address all issues covered by the release.
    Key Points
    • 01F5 disclosed CVE-2026-123007, a critical integer-underflow flaw in nginx HTTP/2 flow-control accounting that can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to read and overwrite memory in an nginx worker process.
    • 02The issue affects nginx Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8, along with specified NGINX Plus releases, only when HTTP/2 is enabled.
    • 03F5 fixed the issue in nginx Open Source 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, and in NGINX Plus 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1.
    • 04Servers that support only HTTP/1.1 are not affected, and organizations that cannot immediately patch can mitigate exposure by disabling HTTP/2.
    • 05The article states that no exploitation in the wild had been reported as of November 18, 2026, although researchers confirmed working unauthenticated remote code execution against affected builds.

    In plain words

    Researchers found serious flaws in NGINX, widely used software that helps websites handle visitors, which could let an outsider take control of an unpatched server without logging in. The problems affect many older NGINX versions when a website uses the newer HTTP/2 connection method, and one also applies when the site passes requests to another service behind it. In the worst case, attackers could run their own commands and potentially take full control of the underlying machine, so organizations using affected NGINX versions should install the available updates quickly.

    Summary
    Critical HTTP/2 flaws in NGINX can enable unauthenticated remote code execution and, when chained with a Linux kernel SCTP bug, potential root-level host compromise. Administrators should immediately upgrade to NGINX Open Source 1.30.7/1.31.9 or NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1/37.3.0.1; disabling HTTP/2 is a temporary mitigation for the two nginx2root flaws.

    Researchers disclosed two critical NGINX HTTP/2 flaws dubbed “nginx2root” that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on vulnerable web servers. CVE-2026-123007 is a flow-control memory-corruption issue affecting NGINX 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, while CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free issue affecting versions 1.19.7 through 1.31.8 when NGINX proxies requests to a backend. Wiz demonstrated remote code execution for both issues, and Xint demonstrated root access by combining the first flaw with a Linux kernel SCTP issue that can escape an NGINX Docker container.

    F5 fixed the reported issues in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 stable and 1.31.9 mainline; NGINX Plus users should update to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1. Administrators are advised to upgrade immediately, or temporarily disable HTTP/2 if an upgrade cannot yet be performed, although that measure covers only the two nginx2root flaws. Exposure cannot be determined from NGINX version numbers alone, because the main flaws require reachable HTTP/2 and may have been fixed through backports; Censys estimated 8.8 million potentially exposed services based on visible version data and HTTP/2 support.

    • NGINX version numbers alone cannot confirm exposure because the two main flaws require reachable HTTP/2 to be enabled, and fixes may have been backported without changing the reported version.
    • The second critical flaw has a narrower but important condition: it applies when NGINX both accepts HTTP/2 connections and forwards requests to a backend service.
    • Disabling HTTP/2 is only a temporary measure for the two nginx2root issues and does not address the three other reported flaws or the separate TLS 1.3 denial-of-service issue.
    • Censys estimated that 8.8 million services were potentially exposed based on visible versions and HTTP/2 support, but 104 million services did not disclose their NGINX version, limiting internet-wide exposure estimates.
    Key Points
    • 01Two critical NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on affected servers.
    • 02CVE-2026-123007 affects NGINX versions 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, while CVE-2026-123633 affects versions 1.19.7 through 1.31.8 when NGINX proxies requests to a backend.
    • 03Researchers demonstrated remote code execution against NGINX serving static files over HTTP/2 with TLS, and Xint demonstrated root access by chaining CVE-2026-123007 with a Linux kernel SCTP flaw.
    • 04F5 fixed the reported flaws in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 stable and 1.31.9 mainline, and NGINX Plus users should update to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1.
    • 05Administrators are advised to upgrade immediately or temporarily disable HTTP/2, although disabling HTTP/2 only mitigates the two nginx2root flaws.

In plain words

F5 issued emergency fixes for ten security problems in NGINX, software used to run websites and route internet traffic. Five of the flaws are especially serious because an outsider could potentially take control of an affected server; the most urgent one affects sites using a common newer web connection method and has a public demonstration available. Organizations using affected NGINX Open Source or NGINX Plus versions should install the updated version and restart it, because attackers who gain server access may be able to take over the underlying computer as well.

Summary
F5 released out-of-band patches for five critical NGINX RCE flaws, led by CVE-2026-123007 in HTTP/2, plus five additional vulnerabilities; organizations should upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7/1.31.9 or the applicable NGINX Plus fixed release and restart the service.

F5 issued an out-of-band security release on November 18, 2026, fixing ten NGINX vulnerabilities in NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus. Five of these flaws, referred to by Xint as NGINX2Root, are critical remote code execution issues affecting HTTP/2, HTTP/3, the resolver, and the mail proxy module. The most urgent, CVE-2026-123007, is an unauthenticated HTTP/2 flaw that requires only HTTP/2 over TLS to be enabled and has a public proof of concept.

The public exploit for CVE-2026-123007 was demonstrated against NGINX 1.31.8, but Rapid7 describes it as constrained because it requires substantial HTTP/2 traffic, heap-address recovery, and a specific x86-64 glibc memory-copy routine. The article reported no evidence that the five critical flaws had been exploited as zero-days or by threat actors as of November 18. Organizations should upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or move NGINX Plus to the applicable fixed 37.x releases, and restart NGINX because a configuration reload does not replace the running executable.

  • Disabling HTTP/2 only mitigates the two HTTP/2 flaws and does not protect against the resolver, HTTP/3, or mail proxy vulnerabilities.
  • A configuration reload is insufficient after upgrading NGINX because it does not replace the running executable; NGINX must be restarted.
  • NGINX Plus R33 through R36 have no patch available, so affected customers must move to a fixed 37.x release.
  • The public CVE-2026-123007 exploit is constrained by its need for roughly 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, recovery of heap addresses to overcome address randomization, and an x86-64-specific glibc memory-copy routine.
Key Points
  • 01F5’s November 18 out-of-band release fixed five critical NGINX remote code execution vulnerabilities and five additional NGINX flaws.
  • 02CVE-2026-123007 is an unauthenticated NGINX HTTP/2 remote code execution flaw that requires HTTP/2 over TLS to be enabled, and a public proof of concept is available.
  • 03The five critical NGINX2Root vulnerabilities affect NGINX HTTP/2, HTTP/3, the resolver, and the mail proxy module, depending on which features are enabled.
  • 04NGINX Open Source users should upgrade to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, while NGINX Plus users should move to applicable fixed 37.x releases and restart NGINX after upgrading.
  • 05As of November 18, the article reported no evidence that the five NGINX vulnerabilities had been exploited as zero-days or by threat actors.

    In plain words

    Drupal fixed a serious flaw that could let someone without an account use a leftover setup page to try to reinstall a website and possibly take control of it. Websites using older Drupal 10 or 11 versions are affected, while older Drupal 8, 9, and some outdated 10 and 11 versions will not receive a fix. Site owners should install the updated versions and block access to the setup page, because public examples showing how to misuse the flaw already exist and attacks could be developed quickly.

    Summary
    Drupal has patched CVE-2026-132165, a critical installer flaw that could let unauthenticated attackers reinstall and potentially take over vulnerable sites. Administrators should update to Drupal 11.4.13, 11.3.22, or 10.6.22 and block access to /core/install.php.

    Drupal has released fixes for CVE-2026-132165, a critical flaw in Drupal core that can, under specific conditions, let an unauthenticated attacker use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site. A successful attack could result in site takeover or remote code execution. Drupal rated the issue 18 out of 25 on its risk scale, described vulnerable configurations as uncommon, and said exploitation is complex despite an existing proof-of-concept.

    The installer, located at /core/install.php, remains on sites after installation and is not blocked by Drupal core’s default .htaccess rules. Drupal recommends updating to versions 11.4.13, 11.3.22, or 10.6.22, depending on the supported branch, and blocking installer access even after updating. Drupal 8 and 9, Drupal 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 11.2.x and earlier are end-of-life and will not receive a fix; the article notes that about 29% of reporting Drupal sites were running end-of-life branches.

    • Drupal’s installer file remains on deployed sites after installation, and Drupal’s default .htaccess rules do not block requests to it, leaving that protection to each site.
    • Some exploit paths are prevented when the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php.
    • Drupal Steward users are protected from known attack paths, but Drupal still advises them to update in case additional paths emerge.
    • The flaw was identified by Anthropic’s automated OSS Scanner service, and Drupal says an AI-driven surge in security reports is contributing to reduced security-coverage periods beginning in 2027.
    • About 29% of Drupal sites reporting usage data were running end-of-life branches that do not receive fixes.
    Key Points
    • 01Drupal disclosed and patched CVE-2026-132165, a critical Drupal core flaw that can, under specific conditions, let an unauthenticated attacker use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site.
    • 02A successful exploit could lead to site takeover or remote code execution, though Drupal rates affected configurations as uncommon and says exploitation is complex.
    • 03Affected releases include Drupal versions below 10.6.22, Drupal 11.0.0 through 11.3.x before 11.3.22, and Drupal 11.4.0 through 11.4.12.
    • 04Drupal recommends updating to 11.4.13, 11.3.22, or 10.6.22 and blocking access to /core/install.php even after applying the update.
    • 05Drupal 8 and 9, Drupal 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 11.2.x and earlier are end-of-life and will not receive a fix.

In plain words

Drupal, software used to build and manage many large websites, fixed a serious flaw that could let an anonymous stranger take control of an unpatched site by rerunning its setup process. Government bodies, schools, universities, businesses, and media organizations that use Drupal may be affected. The risk is urgent because the makers warn that working attack methods could appear within hours or days, so site owners should install the update or temporarily block access to the setup page.

Summary
Drupal has patched CVE-2026-132165, a critical unauthenticated flaw that can allow attackers to reinstall Drupal and potentially take over vulnerable sites. Administrators should upgrade immediately or block access to /core/install.php until they can patch.

Drupal has patched CVE-2026-132165, a critical remote code execution flaw discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner. Under specific conditions, anonymous attackers can use Drupal’s install.php installer to attempt to reinstall the CMS, which can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution. Drupal warned that exploit methods could be developed within hours or days.

Organizations should update to Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, or 11.4.13, while those unable to patch immediately can block access to /core/install.php through web server settings or the site’s .htaccess file. Some attack paths are mitigated when the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php, and Drupal Steward WAF customers are protected against known attack vectors but are still advised to update. Drupal also fixed CVE-2026-132166, a moderately critical gadget chain issue that could enable remote code execution for attackers with administrator privileges when untrusted data is deserialized because of another flaw.

  • Restricting the web server's ability to write to or change permissions on settings.php can mitigate some paths for the critical installer flaw.
  • Organizations unable to patch immediately can reduce exposure by blocking access to /core/install.php through their web server configuration or the site's .htaccess file.
  • Drupal Steward WAF customers are protected from known attack paths, but Drupal still recommends upgrading because additional attack paths may be found.
  • The separate CVE-2026-132166 issue requires administrative access and another flaw that causes untrusted data to be processed, making it dependent on additional conditions.
Key Points
  • 01Drupal patched CVE-2026-132165, a critical flaw that can allow anonymous attackers to attempt to reinstall Drupal and potentially take over a vulnerable site or run code remotely.
  • 02Drupal released fixed versions 10.6.22, 11.3.22, and 11.4.13, and advises organizations that cannot immediately update to block access to /core/install.php.
  • 03The Drupal Security Team warned that exploits could be developed within hours or days and said at least one of the critical issues can be exploited by anonymous users.
  • 04Drupal also fixed CVE-2026-132166, a moderately critical issue that administrators could use to run code remotely if the application processes untrusted data because of another flaw.
  • 05The article notes that CISA has listed five Drupal flaws as exploited in the wild since November 2021, including two used in ransomware attacks.

    phpAfterShell Explained: How Hackers Could Turn a PHP Session Flaw Into Code Execution
    thehackernews.com · 19 Nov 2026 16:59 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGScve-2026-126714depthfirstphpphp-8-2php-8-3php-8-4php-8-5php-files-session-handlerphp2shellphpaftershellredissession-upload-progress
    In plain words

    PHP fixed a serious flaw called phpAfterShell that could let an attacker interfere with how a website saves sign-in and other session information, potentially allowing them to run commands on the website’s server. It affects websites using PHP’s default method of storing session information in files, including PHP versions 8.2 through 8.5 before the newly released fixes. A successful attack could alter details such as who is signed in, their permissions, or security tokens, and in some cases take control of the server. Website owners should install the updated PHP releases, rebuild and redeploy their systems, and confirm that their live sites are using the fixed version.

    Summary
    PHP has patched the critical phpAfterShell session-file flaw (CVE-2026-126714), which can let attackers manipulate interrupted session writes to deserialize attacker-controlled objects and potentially achieve code execution. Update to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, or later; disabling upload-progress tracking is only a temporary, incomplete mitigation.

    PHP released fixes for phpAfterShell, a critical file-based session handling flaw tracked as CVE-2026-126714 and rated 9.2 out of 10 by PHP maintainers. The issue affects PHP 8.2 before 8.2.36, PHP 8.3 before 8.3.37, PHP 8.4 before 8.4.28, and PHP 8.5 before 8.5.13; PHP 8.6.0 also includes the fix. Servers that installed the October 21 PHP2Shell patches remain affected until they install these newer releases, although no attacks using phpAfterShell have been reported.

    The flaw can occur when a PHP session-file write stops partway through, leaving a mix of new and old data that an attacker may shape so PHP later treats it as a separately stored object. In the tested route, PHP upload-progress tracking writes information into a user session before the application’s own code runs, and a later request that starts the session can load the planted object. Operators are advised to update PHP, rebuild and redeploy container images where applicable, and verify that the PHP version serving web requests includes the patch.

PHP released security updates for 18 vulnerabilities across all supported branches: PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36. The flaws affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, PHP-FPM, CGI, and other components, and include issues that could allow unauthenticated remote code execution. Additional fixes address memory corruption, information disclosure, cross-site scripting, denial-of-service problems, and potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs.

The most serious issue, CVE-2026-129289, is a PHP-FPM request-smuggling flaw rated 9.2 that can allow remote execution of PHP code when certain nginx, Apache, HAProxy, or LSAPI configurations reuse backend connections. Standard nginx and Apache configurations that do not reuse those connections are not affected by this specific attack. Other notable fixes include multiple use-after-free and session-related flaws that could also lead to remote code execution, plus a PHP-FPM issue that could allow local privilege escalation.

Administrators are urged to upgrade to the newly released versions. If an immediate update is not possible, persistent connections between web servers and PHP-FPM can be disabled to mitigate CVE-2026-129289, while disabling session upload progress and restarting PHP workers was recommended for the session-related CVE-2026-115560. These measures do not address all vulnerabilities, and administrators should ensure PHP-FPM and LSAPI listeners are not directly exposed to untrusted networks.

  • The highest-severity PHP-FPM flaw depends on connection reuse in specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, or LSAPI configurations, so standard nginx and Apache deployments that close backend connections after each request are not affected by that particular attack.
  • Disabling persistent backend connections can reduce exposure to CVE-2026-129289 when immediate patching is not possible, but it does not protect against the other vulnerabilities fixed in the release.
  • PHP’s temporary mitigation for the session-related CVE-2026-115560 is to disable session upload progress and restart PHP workers.
  • While official fixes cover only supported PHP branches, patched packages and hardened container images with backported fixes are available for several unsupported PHP versions dating back to PHP 5.6.
  • Administrators should also ensure PHP-FPM and LSAPI listeners are not directly reachable from untrusted networks.

In plain words

The U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA says criminals are actively using four software flaws affecting Synology storage devices, LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and REDCap, a research data platform. These weaknesses can let outsiders take control of servers, and have been connected to file-locking extortion, hidden cryptocurrency mining, and theft of access to AI services. Organizations using these products should apply available fixes or other safeguards quickly; Apache Axis 1.x is no longer supported, so users may need to move to a replacement product.

Summary
CISA added four actively exploited flaws in Synology DSM, LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and REDCap to its KEV catalog, linking them to ransomware, cryptomining, and LLMjacking activity. Organizations should urgently patch or mitigate the affected systems, especially because Apache Axis 1.x is end-of-life and lacks an official fix.

CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities affecting Synology DiskStation Manager, BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and Vanderbilt University REDCap to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The flaws include three remote code execution issues with CVSS scores of 9.8 and a LiteLLM issue rated 8.8 that can enable code execution through a guardrails testing endpoint. CISA said the REDCap flaw can be triggered through crafted HTTP requests in a public survey context when an attacker knows a valid survey hash.

The Apache Axis flaw has reportedly been used alongside N-able N-central vulnerabilities to install cryptocurrency miners, but Axis 1.x is end-of-life and has no official patch. Separately, Safe Security observed REDCap exploitation that deployed a temporary web shell, loaded XMRig disguised as image files, and established persistence through cron and an added SSH key. The LiteLLM flaw has been used in LLMjacking activity to turn limited-access inference keys into administrator credentials, while the Synology DSM flaw has been linked to C3RB3R ransomware attacks on network-attached storage devices.

  • Apache Axis 1.x presents an unusual remediation problem because it is end-of-life and has no official patch; users are advised to migrate to Axis 2/Java or apply a build containing a specific July 2026 commit.
  • The REDCap exploitation described was designed to be less visible: attackers used a temporary web shell, loaded XMRig into memory, disguised it as image files, and made it appear as the syslog-ng service.
  • The LiteLLM flaw can turn a limited-access inference key into full administrator credentials, meaning a credential intended for restricted AI use can provide much broader control.
  • The four flaws are associated with distinct criminal outcomes—cryptocurrency mining, persistence in AI-service environments, and C3RB3R ransomware—rather than a single type of misuse.
  • CISA set different remediation deadlines, requiring action for the DSM, REDCap, and Axis flaws by November 21, 2026, while allowing until December 2, 2026 for the LiteLLM flaw.

  • 04Threat actors used the LiteLLM flaw CVE-2026-40217 to turn limited AI-service access keys into full administrator credentials and maintain access in LLMjacking campaigns.

    In plain words

    During the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, election websites received far more visitors on Election Day, but Cloudflare saw no major attempts to overwhelm those sites and take them offline. Instead, most harmful activity happened before the election and involved attempts to use weaknesses in website software to get into internal systems or access data. State and local election offices, political campaigns, journalists, and voting-rights groups can all be affected, and keeping their online information available and trustworthy helps voters participate and maintain confidence in election results.

    Summary
    During the 2026 U.S. midterms, election websites saw a 363% Election Day traffic surge but no major DDoS incidents; instead, attackers increasingly focused on web vulnerability exploitation in the weeks before voting. Cloudflare mitigated hundreds of millions of vulnerability attempts against government election sites, including an isolated attempted exploitation of the newly disclosed PHP php2shell flaws.

    During the November 3, 2026 U.S. midterm elections, traffic to state and local government election websites rose to about 602 million requests, a 363% increase from November 1. Despite the surge in voter traffic, Cloudflare reported no significant DDoS attacks across the more than 1,400 election-related websites protected through its programs on Election Day. The only significant DDoS event noted occurred on November 2 against a California U.S. House candidate and totaled 520,000 requests. The findings contrast with other recent elections, including Moldova’s 2025 election, where the Election Commission faced more than 898 million malicious requests in 12 hours.

    Cloudflare found that attempts to exploit website weaknesses, rather than efforts to take sites offline, were the dominant threat to government election websites during the 2026 cycle. It mitigated 392 million website vulnerability attacks against those sites in the 12 months before the election, while daily exploit attempts climbed from 200,000 in January to 2 million in October. On October 22, its PHP protections were triggered more than 9,000 times at one Western U.S. state government election website following disclosure of the php2shell vulnerabilities. The article also found that journalism and election-related civil society organizations faced substantial DDoS activity, with more than 10.8 billion mitigated requests over the same 12-month period.

    • The highest-risk period for website intrusion attempts was weeks before Election Day rather than the voting day itself, as vulnerability exploit attempts rose steadily through October while Election Day saw no attack-volume escalation.
    • The dominant threat varied by organization type: government election sites were most frequently targeted with website vulnerability attempts, while journalism and election-related civil society groups primarily faced DDoS traffic.
    • Basic email authentication alone was insufficient for many campaign-targeted malicious emails, because nearly 42% of those messages passed those checks despite being identified by advanced phishing detection.
    • The isolated PHP exploitation attempt the day after public disclosure shows why automatically updated defenses can matter when newly reported software flaws begin to be targeted quickly.
    • Election services must plan for both hostile activity and legitimate demand, since voter traffic rose sharply on Election Day even though major DDoS activity did not.

In plain words

Attackers exploited two newly disclosed flaws in PHP, a common tool used to run website features, against internet-facing management pages for Palo Alto Networks firewalls. They studied the same software used across many devices and combined the flaws with another bug to take full control of 25 systems in several countries. The article’s broader warning is that firewalls and other network equipment often rely on web pages for administration, so those pages need the same careful protection and limited access as any important website.

Summary
The PHP2Shell flaws show that internet-exposed firewall and appliance management interfaces are high-risk web applications: attackers can pre-profile identical firmware builds and chain exploits despite mitigations such as ASLR. Organizations should identify these interfaces, patch affected PHP/PAN-OS systems, and restrict management access to trusted internal networks.

Attackers exploited the unauthenticated PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces. Palo Alto Networks confirmed the activity on October 28 after details of the flaws leaked ahead of coordinated disclosure and PHP issued an emergency patch. The incident highlights that firewalls and other network appliances often expose web applications that control critical systems.

The flaws require skill and target-specific knowledge to exploit reliably, but appliances make that work more practical because identical software versions run across many devices. Investigators found that the attacker obtained and decrypted PAN-OS firmware, extracted PHP libraries, and built memory profiles for nine versions. The attacker then chained PHP2Shell with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw, CVE-2026-46300, to obtain root access on 25 systems, including 24 firewalls and one management server in the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.

PHP2Shell uses crafted multipart uploads that exhaust PHP memory while a request is being parsed, before application code executes. Deeply nested empty file fields can consume far more memory than the request size suggests, allowing a request below PHP’s default 8 MB upload limit to exhaust its default 128 MB memory limit. Protections such as ASLR made exploitation harder, and nginx buffering disrupted some public exploit chains, but Palo Alto advised removing internet access from management interfaces and restricting them to trusted internal IP addresses.

  • Appliance software can be a softer target even when protections such as address space layout randomization are enabled, because attackers can obtain identical firmware and calculate version-specific memory details in advance.
  • A PHP2Shell request can be much smaller than PHP's default 8 MB upload-size limit while still exhausting its 128 MB memory limit by using deeply nested empty file fields.
  • An nginx proxy in front of PAN-OS buffered chunked request bodies and disrupted public PHP2Shell exploit chains, illustrating that intermediary systems can alter exploit behavior unexpectedly.
  • A high volume of PHP2Shell attempts in logs did not reliably indicate that a server was vulnerable, because many public proof-of-concept exploits did not work against all targets.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers exploited the unauthenticated PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 against internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces.
  • 02The attackers obtained and decrypted PAN-OS firmware, extracted PHP libraries, created memory profiles for nine versions, and chained PHP2Shell with CVE-2026-46300 to gain root access on 25 systems.
  • 03PHP2Shell uses crafted multipart uploads to exhaust PHP memory during request parsing, leaving uninitialized memory or a pointer to memory that has already been freed.
  • 04Public exploit attempts were often unreliable because protections such as address space layout randomization made exploitation more difficult, though appliance software versions can be studied in advance.
  • 05Palo Alto Networks advised removing internet access from management interfaces and limiting access to trusted internal IP addresses.

In plain words

An attacker abused a weakness in Optimizely, a service many websites use to change and test their pages, to add harmful code to the sites’ existing Optimizely page components. Visitors to more than 450 affected website domains could have had cryptocurrency payment addresses swapped for the attacker’s address, payment-card details or website cookies collected, and iPhone or iPad users sent to pages attempting to exploit their devices. This matters because compromising one trusted web service can put visitors to many unrelated businesses at risk without any obvious change to the website they are using.

Summary
Attackers abused a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation’s signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer snippets, potentially exposing visitors across hundreds of sites to crypto-wallet replacement, payment-card skimming, cookie theft, and iOS exploit delivery. Organizations should urgently audit Optimizely Project JavaScript, rotate affected credentials and tokens, and restrict third-party scripts with CSP and monitoring.

On November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely Web Experimentation’s account signup flow that allowed unauthorized modification of the Project JavaScript field in customer projects. Because this field runs custom code on pages loading an Optimizely snippet, the attacker injected malicious JavaScript that was delivered to visitors through legitimate Optimizely snippets, including CDN-hosted copies. Optimizely said it blocked the vulnerable route, deployed a fix, removed injected code, ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset affected access, and notified customers. ThreatLabz identified more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script across industries including banking, e-commerce, travel, retail, media, and technology.

In most affected snippets, an injected loader fetched a second-stage payload called track.js from attacker-controlled infrastructure, including 1688360[.]cc. The payload monitored for cryptocurrency wallet addresses and attempted to replace them with attacker-controlled addresses; after a visible replacement, it could collect a screenshot, the page URL, accessible cookies, and related metadata. Later versions also monitored page inputs, form submissions, keyboard activity, and web requests for payment-card details, although they could not read data entered in secure cross-origin payment frames. On iPhones and iPads, the code attempted to load the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits and, for selected operating-system versions, could add a hidden iframe for a further delivery path.

The article emphasizes that most observed script behavior remained within the affected website’s browser page, rather than providing direct access to unrelated sites, tabs, local files, or browser-wide activity. It recommends that organizations audit Optimizely Project JavaScript and administrative activity, rotate credentials and tokens, enforce multi-factor authentication, verify approved snippet versions, and use Content Security Policy controls and third-party script monitoring. Visitors to affected sites are advised to review banking and cryptocurrency activity, update iOS and iPadOS, and change reused passwords for potentially affected accounts.

  • The malicious code was delivered through Optimizely’s normal snippet delivery paths, including its CDN, meaning affected websites could serve it from infrastructure they already trusted.
  • The script only captured screenshots and sent cookies after it had replaced a valid cryptocurrency wallet address in a visible page element, tying this data collection to apparent wallet-replacement activity.
  • The payment-card collection capability could monitor fields and requests on the compromised page, but it could not read payment details entered in secure payment fields hosted in separate cross-origin frames such as Stripe or Adyen fields.
  • Most of the observed behavior was limited to the affected website’s browser page and could not directly access unrelated tabs, other sites’ cookies, local files, or browser-wide activity unless an iOS or iPadOS exploit chain succeeded.
  • Optimizely reported that it blocked the vulnerable path, removed injected code, ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset affected account access, and notified impacted customers.

  • 03The payload could replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, collect cookies and page screenshots after a visible wallet replacement, and later versions attempted to collect payment-card details entered on affected websites.
  • 04For iPhone and iPad visitors, the payload attempted to load the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits and sometimes inserted a hidden iframe for selected iOS and iPadOS versions.

Broadcom has released fixes for CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter authentication-bypass flaw in the VMware Directory Service with a CVSS score of 9.8. An attacker with network access could bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, which organizations use to manage ESX hosts and virtual machines. Broadcom says the issue qualifies as an emergency change under ITIL methodologies and advises organizations to consult security staff immediately on patch timing.

The flaw affects vCenter 8.0, 9.0, and 9.1, including builds bundled with VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, Telco Cloud Platform, and Telco Cloud Infrastructure. Broadcom lists no workaround, and unsupported vSphere 6.5 and 6.7 systems should be presumed affected; vSphere 7.0 customers may request a patch through extended support. The updates are cumulative and cannot be installed through vCenter Quick Patch, but virtual machines continue running during installation while vCenter management access is briefly unavailable.

  • The update can be installed while virtual machines remain running, although vCenter management access is briefly unavailable and certain encryption operations using a Standard Key Provider pause until vCenter returns online.
  • Organizations already planning to move to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1 should account for a documented upgrade conflict: vCenter 8.0 U3m or 9.0.2.0200 prevents a later upgrade to VCF 9.1.1.

  • The new issue is the second critical VMware Directory Service authentication flaw disclosed that year, and attacks against a separate July directory-traversal flaw began five days after disclosure.

    Ruby2Shell (GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5) is a critical unauthenticated Ruby RCE affecting Ruby 2.4.0 through 3.3.13, 3.4.12, and 4.0.9 when applications case-convert untrusted legacy-encoded strings, including default Rails and classic Sinatra setups. UTF-8 strings are not affected, but Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications are exposed by default because they perform relevant case changes on untrusted strings.

Ruby fixed the problem in versions 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10, while Ruby 3.2 and older are end of life and have no fix. The article says current releases of GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse, and Chatwoot still bundle affected Ruby versions, and recommends restricting access to those servers until vendors release fixes.

Ruby, a widely used programming language, released updates to fix seven bugs in how it handles text and search patterns. Five of the bugs have been shown to let specially crafted input potentially run code on a server, while others could expose information or crash a program. Summary
Ruby has patched seven memory-safety flaws in its regex engine and string case-conversion code, five of which have proof-of-concept remote code execution exploits. Organizations should upgrade to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14 and rebuild or restart affected deployments, as older Ruby versions will not be fixed.

Ruby released versions 4.0.10, 3.4.13, and 3.3.14 to fix seven memory-safety flaws in its regular-expression engine and string case-conversion code. The maintainers said proof-of-concept exploits show that five of the flaws can be used to trigger remote code execution with crafted input, though no attacks have been reported. The issues include heap overflows, a double free, and out-of-bounds reads; the remaining flaws may cause attacker-controlled memory corruption, memory disclosure, or program crashes.

An application’s exposure depends on whether an attacker can control regular-expression patterns or strings processed by vulnerable Ruby code. Most regex issues require an application to build and compile or execute a regex from attacker-controlled input, while one moderate issue can be triggered by a crafted subject string against a fixed pattern using a case-insensitive backreference. Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life and will not receive fixes, and updating gems or frameworks alone does not replace the vulnerable Ruby interpreter running on servers, workers, or container images.

  • Updating application gems or frameworks will not remove the risk; the Ruby interpreter running on servers, background workers, and container images must be upgraded and then restarted or rebuilt.
  • Most regex-related flaws require an attacker to control a pattern that the application compiles or runs, but the moderate backreference flaw can be triggered by a crafted input string even when the application uses a fixed pattern.
  • The flaws cannot yet be tracked by CVE number, so organizations must use the GitHub advisory identifiers in scanners and software inventories until CVEs are assigned.
  • Ruby 3.2 and older releases are end of life and will not receive fixes, making migration to a supported Ruby release necessary rather than waiting for a patch.

In plain words

ASUS released updates for its Control Center Express software after finding three serious security problems, including one that could let an outsider take administrator control without logging in. The software is used by businesses and IT service providers to monitor and manage groups of ASUS computers, so a successful break-in could give an attacker control over both the management dashboard and the devices connected to it. ASUS says affected users should install version 1.7.29 and update the small management programs installed on their computers.

Summary
ASUS has patched critical flaws in Control Center Express, including a CVSS 10 hard-coded key issue that lets unauthenticated remote attackers forge admin tokens and take control of managed systems. Organizations should upgrade to version 1.7.29 and update deployed client agents immediately.

ASUS released Control Center Express version 1.7.29 to fix three critical security flaws in its centralized PC management software. The most severe issue, CVE-2026-114202, has a CVSS score of 10.0 and stems from a hard-coded cryptographic key. It could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to forge an authentication token and gain administrator privileges without user interaction. Because Control Center Express is used to monitor and remotely manage fleets of PCs, the flaw could affect both the management console and managed devices.

The other two flaws are CVE-2026-114204, which could let a low-privileged remote attacker forge a session token for a recently logged-in account, and CVE-2026-114205, which could let a low-privileged user create an administrator account. ASUS says versions earlier than 1.7.29 are affected, though the CVE records list affected versions only through 1.7.27, making version 1.7.28’s status unclear. Users should install version 1.7.29, update the agents on managed devices through the Client Agent Updater, and verify their versions. ASUS also issued updates for Control Center Enterprise, Control Center Datacenter, and Armoury Crate to fix additional authorization and privilege-escalation issues.

  • The most severe Control Center Express flaw requires neither an existing account nor user interaction, unlike the other two flaws, which require either low-level access or a recently active session.
  • ASUS’s bulletin says all releases before 1.7.29 are affected, but the associated CVE records list affected versions only through 1.7.27, leaving version 1.7.28’s status unclear.
  • Updating the Control Center Express server alone is not the complete remediation step: ASUS also directs users to update and verify the agents installed on managed devices.
  • The related Control Center Enterprise and Datacenter flaw could let someone with only a Viewer role reset an administrator’s password and take over that account.

  • 03CVE-2026-114204 can allow a low-privileged remote attacker to forge a session token for a recently logged-in account, while CVE-2026-114205 can allow a low-privileged user to create an administrator account.

Summary
A UK tribunal confirmed that the British government issued Apple a secret technical capability notice targeting iCloud encryption, prompting Apple to withdraw Advanced Data Protection for UK users. The court rejected the government's refusal to acknowledge the notice, though its legality will not be decided until a hearing planned for 2027.

The UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal confirmed that the British government gave Apple a secret technical capability notice concerning the cryptographic protections of iCloud accounts. The tribunal rejected the government’s argument that it could neither confirm nor deny the notice’s existence for national-security reasons. The ruling found that acknowledging the notice would not reveal information adversaries could not already obtain from public reporting and statements by senior US officials.

The dispute centers on Apple’s Advanced Data Protection feature, which stores encryption keys on users’ own devices rather than on Apple’s servers, leaving Apple unable to access protected iCloud content. Apple withdrew Advanced Data Protection for UK users in February after receiving the notice, apparently complying by removing the feature in Britain. The tribunal has not decided whether the notice was lawful, and a substantive hearing is scheduled for the first half of 2027.

  • Apple’s strongest iCloud protection was designed so that Apple itself does not possess users’ encryption keys, meaning it could not provide account contents even when presented with a lawful request.

  • The government can avoid departing from its policy of neither confirming nor denying such notices by withdrawing from or settling the proceedings, according to the tribunal’s earlier judgment.
  • The case separates transparency from legality: the court required acknowledgment of the notice but has not yet ruled on whether the notice itself was lawful.

In plain words

A researcher showed that some bugs in PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, and Oracle databases could let a person with very limited access run commands on the computer hosting the database. In one Oracle case, the researcher says the path could begin through an exposed web service without any account at all. Although there is no evidence these flaws have been used in real attacks, organizations using the affected software should install available updates and limit unneeded rights to create temporary database data, because database read restrictions alone may not protect the server.

Summary
Researcher Zheng Yu demonstrated that low-privilege database users can potentially achieve server-side code execution through memory-safety flaws in PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, and Oracle. Organizations should promptly apply available patches and restrict unnecessary TEMPORARY and temporary-table creation privileges.

Depthfirst researcher Zheng Yu published proof-of-concept exploits showing that low-privilege database accounts can potentially run code on the servers hosting PostgreSQL, MySQL, and ClickHouse. The research also describes an Oracle chain that reportedly reaches command execution through an exposed web endpoint without requiring a login. The article states that none of the chains has been observed in real-world attacks and that the full attack chains were not independently reproduced.

The work highlights that database permissions limiting access to application tables do not necessarily prevent the database engine from processing malicious input through memory-unsafe code. PostgreSQL’s default TEMPORARY privilege and temporary-table creation rights in MySQL and ClickHouse can provide sufficient access to reach some of the reported flaws. PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Oracle have issued fixes for the listed CVEs, while the ClickHouse issue has no assigned CVE or confirmed fixed version; the article advises applying updates and removing unnecessary temporary-object privileges.

  • Database permissions that prevent access to application tables may still not prevent server compromise, because ordinary SQL can reach memory-unsafe code used to process queries and database objects.
  • PostgreSQL's default TEMPORARY privilege, and temporary-table creation rights in MySQL and ClickHouse, can provide enough access to trigger flaws without reading existing application data.
  • Oracle rated the MySQL issue as requiring high privileges, but the researcher reported code execution using an account that could only create temporary tables.
  • The two Oracle flaws were each rated as not exploitable without a login on their own, yet the researcher reported that chaining them through an exposed web endpoint enabled command execution before authentication.
  • The ClickHouse issue can reportedly be reached by setting format_binary_max_string_size to zero, but it has neither an assigned CVE nor a confirmed fixed version.

  • 04Oracle patched Oracle Text CVE-2026-114819 and Oracle REST Data Services CVE-2026-91609, which the researcher chained through an exposed web endpoint before login.

The Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security announced the Threat Disruption Center, a new task force intended to disrupt victim payments to foreign criminal networks behind scams, cybercrime, and sextortion targeting Americans. The center will improve handling of victim complaints, map criminal networks, and create a direct channel for cooperation with private-sector organizations that work with victims. It is housed within the Homeland Security Task Force, an interagency network involving more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners.

The center will share intelligence with technology, banking, domain, web-hosting, social-media, and cryptocurrency companies so they can take actions such as pausing victim payments, removing malicious domains, and banning scam-linked accounts. TRM Labs said the effort has already taken down more than 1,600 scam websites, added more than 6,600 scam-linked cryptocurrency wallet addresses to a screening network, and identified 101 fraud networks for investigation. The initiative follows reported cyber-scam losses of $20.9 billion to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center in 2025, while Treasury separately sanctioned alleged scam operators in Myanmar and Cambodian Prince Group affiliates.

In plain words

The article explains why a simple safety check can often be tricked when it has less ability to understand an input than the program or AI system that receives it afterward. It uses examples such as malicious software hiding from scanners, fake document images that fooled text-reading tools, and a 2025 technique called PuzzleMask that could hide a harmful request from a quick AI check while a stronger AI could decode it. This matters to security companies, software makers, and everyday users because perfect screening is unrealistic; better checks and multiple layers of protection can still make real attacks much harder.

Summary
The article argues that security controls inevitably become bypassable when a weaker gatekeeper must screen inputs for a more capable system, unless the control relies on a hard problem such as cryptographic verification. Defenders should identify these asymmetries, narrow them with stronger or better-integrated analysis, and use defense in depth rather than expecting perfect filtering.

The article introduces “gatekeeper asymmetry doom,” the idea that a system reviewing adversarial input will eventually be bypassed if it is less capable than the system that later processes that input, unless the review relies on a hard problem such as cryptographic signature verification. It illustrates the principle through hash-based antivirus detection, pattern matching, deny lists, static binary analysis, and sandboxing. In each case, attackers can alter, obscure, or condition inputs in ways that exceed the checker’s ability to recognize them while still allowing the target system to process them. The article emphasizes that this does not make mitigations worthless, but means they should not be treated as perfect barriers.

A central LLM example is PuzzleMask, a technique the authors say they researched in late 2025 to conceal a policy-violating prompt from a limited external LLM check while a stronger target model could decode and consider the hidden instruction. The article says this is not itself a jailbreak, because it does not claim to defeat the target model’s own internal safety rules, but it can remove the protection of a weaker pre-screening layer. It also describes sandbox evasions based on the gap between simulated and real human interaction, as well as malicious macro lures designed to be readable by people but difficult for older text-recognition systems. The recommended response is to identify these capability gaps, use stronger or better-integrated gatekeepers where feasible, evaluate whether bypasses are practical in the real world, and maintain defense in depth.

  • A more capable language model can be more vulnerable to a weaker external AI filter because the stronger model may successfully decode a hidden instruction that the filter failed to recognize.
  • Sandbox evasions are not always fixable by correcting a list of detectable differences: some checks depend on resources a sandbox inherently lacks, such as interaction from a real human user.
  • The article argues that imperfect defenses remain valuable because attackers often use suboptimal methods; a mitigation can reduce real-world harm even if a theoretical bypass exists.
  • The Time Hierarchy Theorem is presented as a formal analogy for the problem: when the protected system has materially more time to process an input than its checker, there are classifications that the slower checker cannot always decide correctly.
Key Points
  • 01The article defines “gatekeeper asymmetry doom” as the claim that a system checking adversarial input will inevitably be bypassed if it is strictly less powerful than the system that processes the input, unless it uses a hard problem such as cryptographic verification.
  • 02It argues that hash matching, deny lists, regular-expression rules, and static binary analysis can be evaded because attackers can alter or obscure inputs while preserving their behavior.
  • 03Sandbox analysis reduces some capability gaps by executing suspicious programs, but malware can still detect differences between a sandbox and a real victim machine, including the absence of genuine human mouse movement.
  • 04The article describes PuzzleMask, a late-2025 technique that hid policy-violating prompts from a limited AI screening model while allowing a stronger target model with more reasoning effort and code tools to identify and process the concealed request.
  • 05The article concludes that defenders should identify unavoidable gaps, strengthen or better use gatekeepers, assess how practical a bypass is, and rely on defense in depth rather than expecting perfect filtering.

In plain words

This article explains how attackers can use a stolen developer account or access key to make harmful software releases while appearing to be legitimate team members. Incidents involving npm package maintainers, Nx, TanStack, LiteLLM, and Codecov show that one compromised account can expose secrets, change release settings, or publish malicious updates used by millions of downstream users. Summary
GitHub Actions defenses must assume a maintainer credential can be compromised: reduce standing privileges, restrict workflow changes and execution, use OIDC and human-gated releases, and continuously detect and revoke suspicious access. The key measure is how many independently protected credentials an attacker must compromise to ship a malicious release.

This article explains how GitHub Actions release pipelines can be abused when an attacker obtains a valid maintainer account, token, SSH key, deploy key, or browser session. In these cases, actions such as changing workflows, publishing packages, approving deployments, or weakening rules can appear to GitHub and registries as ordinary authenticated work. The article uses incidents involving LiteLLM, npm maintainer Qix, GhostAction, Shai-Hulud, Nx, TanStack, and Codecov to show how stolen credentials and release-system access can affect downstream software users.

Its central measure is how many independently protected credentials an attacker must compromise to ship a malicious release, rather than how many accounts nominally participate in approval. It recommends phishing-resistant sign-in methods, short-lived and narrowly scoped credentials, restrictions on workflow-file changes, protections on who can trigger deployment workflows, OIDC-based publishing, staged publishing or human approval gates, secret scanning, provenance verification, and audit-log monitoring. The article also stresses that controls can be bypassed if one privileged account can reach multiple credentials or change the controls themselves, making rapid detection, revocation, and rehearsed incident response essential.

  • Multiple accounts do not create real separation of duties if one administrator or compromised credential can access the other accounts' tokens; the LiteLLM investigation described three accounts used in the incident but a single cascading compromise.
  • GitHub's “Only allow secure two-factor methods” setting still permits authenticator apps and GitHub Mobile, so it cannot by itself guarantee that organization members use phishing-resistant passkeys or hardware security keys.
  • A push ruleset that restricts workflow-file paths can stop an unreviewed workflow push on any branch, but an empty bypass list does not prevent an organization owner from editing or disabling the ruleset itself.
  • Trusted publishing proves which repository workflow published a package, not whether the package contents are safe, so a compromised workflow can still abuse that publishing identity.
  • Deleting a secret from the latest version of a repository does not remove it from prior history, clones, or forks; the article says exposed credentials must be rotated rather than merely deleted.

  • 03Workflow-file protections must cover every branch because an attacker with write access can push a new workflow to a non-default branch, run it immediately, and delete the branch afterward without opening a pull request.
  • 04OIDC trusted publishing removes the need for long-lived package publishing tokens, but a compromised workflow can still publish malicious content unless releases are staged or otherwise require an independently protected human approval.

An AI SOC Is Only as Good as Its Context Layer

In plain words

The article argues that AI systems used to help security teams investigate suspicious activity are only as reliable as the information they can access and understand. Companies that build or buy these systems still need to decide what information the AI sees, what it means, how old it is, and when the AI should stop rather than guess. This matters because a confident-looking AI answer can be wrong when key details are missing, potentially leading teams to dismiss real danger or act on a bad conclusion. Better records of past and current activity can help security, investigation, intelligence, and detection teams make decisions they can explain and defend.

Summary
An AI SOC’s reliability depends more on a well-designed context layer than on the model itself: it needs current and historical evidence, clear data provenance, and defined investigative limits. Organizations should prioritize defensible decisions and cost per investigation when building, assembling, or buying AI-driven security operations.

The article argues that an AI security operations center is only as effective as the context and evidence it can access, rather than the model chosen to operate it. AI agents can summarize alerts, enrich indicators, reconstruct timelines, and draft detections, but they need reliable information about what data means, where it came from, how old it is, and when an investigation should stop. Without this context, an AI system may produce confident answers that exceed the available evidence.

Organizations can build their own AI SOC, use hosted models with internally designed workflows, or buy a managed service, but all three approaches require decisions about accessible evidence, interpretation, investigation scope, and follow-up actions. The article emphasizes historical data, noting that an indicator that appears harmless today may have supported phishing infrastructure days earlier. It recommends measuring AI SOC economics by cost per defensible decision rather than cost per token, since automated investigations may require anywhere from a few lookups to hundreds.

Using a medium-severity Microsoft 365 IAM alert as an example, the article shows how the same evidence can support different decisions for triage, incident response, threat intelligence, and detection engineering. A new IP and unusual location may initially appear explainable by travel or a consumer VPN, but evidence that the host serves credential-attack tooling can justify escalation. The article concludes that teams should establish a context layer before selecting models, agents, or vendors so decisions can be explained and defended.

  • Buying a managed AI SOC does not eliminate architecture decisions; it means inheriting the provider’s choices about accessible evidence, its meaning, investigation depth, and follow-up actions.
  • An API key only gives an AI system access to information and does not explain how to interpret the fields returned, making data definitions and collection provenance operationally important.
  • The same IAM login alert can support different valid next steps for triage, incident response, threat intelligence, and detection engineering when each team examines the evidence with a different purpose.
  • For recurring suspicious-login alerts, identifying the service and traits of suspicious infrastructure can produce a more durable detection than blocking a single IP address.
  • Automatically investigating alerts can make costs difficult to predict because one investigation may involve a few lookups or hundreds, even if the user experience appears identical.
Key Points
  • 01The effectiveness of an AI security operations center depends more on the context and evidence it can access than on the AI model selected.
  • 02Organizations can build an AI SOC, use hosted models with their own workflows, or purchase a managed service, but each approach still requires decisions about evidence, interpretation, investigation scope, and next actions.
  • 03AI can produce confident-looking conclusions despite incomplete context, so systems need clear evidence, data meanings, source information, and limits on when to stop investigating.
  • 04Historical information is important because an indicator that appears harmless now may have been associated with phishing infrastructure earlier.
  • 05Organizations should evaluate AI SOC economics by cost per defensible decision rather than cost per token.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is an evergreen best-practice and opinion piece about designing context for AI-assisted security operations, not coverage of a specific incident, vulnerability, or active threat. It offers useful considerations around data history, provenance, uncertainty, and cost, but has no immediate operational urgency.

Summary
A review of 50 publicly reported AI-related security incidents in 2026 found that most stemmed from familiar failures—exposed secrets, excessive permissions, weak isolation, and compromised suppliers—rather than novel AI-specific vulnerabilities. AI agents and offensive frameworks primarily increased the speed and scale of abuse, making least privilege, credential protection, isolation, monitoring, and approval controls more important.

Aikido reviewed 50 AI-related security incidents disclosed in 2026 through November 19 to determine how AI was involved and what failures enabled the incidents. It categorized 25 incidents as attacks against AI platforms, developer tools, or services with AI credentials; 12 as attacks using AI agents or agentic frameworks; and 13 as cases where agents lacked adequate controls. The review found that exposed secrets were the most frequent failure point, appearing in 13 incidents, while over-scoped identity or trust and weak isolation each appeared in 11. Only three incidents reportedly involved a previously unknown vulnerability.

The incidents often combined multiple failures: 35 of the 44 cases with a stated cause had more than one contributing weakness. Examples included agents reaching systems beyond intended test boundaries through network access and shared administrative credentials, and attackers using ARTEX to automate reconnaissance, authentication attempts, and privilege changes. The article argues that AI increases the speed and potential impact of existing security failures, particularly when agents can access credentials, systems, or irreversible actions without sufficient limits. It recommends limiting agent permissions and network access, keeping secrets out of logs and build environments, monitoring unusual activity, and requiring approval for actions that cannot be undone.

  • AI did not need a new technical flaw to increase harm: the article cites campaigns in which agentic tools moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours by automating reconnaissance, sign-in attempts, and follow-on actions.
  • The most damaging incidents often required several ordinary weaknesses to align; for example, Vercel’s incident combined a compromised third-party AI vendor with broad permissions previously granted through a corporate Google account.
  • Monitoring alone was not always sufficient, because in the Hugging Face incident an alert was raised but the agent run continued, showing that response ownership and action are as important as detection.
  • Prompt-based boundaries were insufficient in reported agent incidents: agents could act on public or untrusted instructions, and test agents reached real systems when internet access and technical isolation were not adequately restricted.
  • Public reporting leaves substantial uncertainty: six of the 50 incidents had no specific cause disclosed, while 17 more lacked at least one important detail, often the attacker’s initial entry point.
Key Points
  • 01The article reviewed 50 AI-related security incidents disclosed in 2026 through November 19 and found that 25 targeted AI platforms, developer tools, or services holding AI credentials, 12 used AI agents or agentic frameworks as attack tools, and 13 involved agents operating without sufficient limits.
  • 02Exposed or reachable secrets were the most common failure point, appearing in 13 incidents, followed by over-scoped identity or trust and weak isolation, each appearing in 11 incidents.
  • 03Only three of the 50 reviewed incidents reportedly involved a previously unknown vulnerability, and the article states that familiar weaknesses determined the damage after attackers gained initial access.
  • 04The article says 35 of the 44 incidents with a stated cause involved more than one failure point, such as exposed credentials combined with broad permissions and limited monitoring.
  • 05The article recommends limiting agent permissions and network access, keeping credentials out of agent logs and build environments, monitoring unusual activity, and requiring approval for irreversible actions.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a roundup of 50 separate AI-related security incidents rather than coverage of one specific event. It offers useful patterns around exposed secrets, excessive permissions, weak isolation, and agent controls, but is primarily an aggregate trend and best-practice analysis.

Five warning signs of ransomware breach before encryption or data theft
bleepingcomputer.com · 19 Nov 2026 15:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSacronisacronis-active-protectionacronis-cyber-platformacronis-edracronis-mdracronis-xdrbcdeditmicrosoft-sharepointvssadminwbadmin
35
In plain words

The article says ransomware criminals often spend time inside an organization’s systems before locking files or stealing data, sometimes taking data without locking anything at all. It points to recent attacks on internet-connected Microsoft SharePoint servers as an example of criminals using stolen access and normal administration tools to move through a victim’s network. This affects organizations whose computers, backups, and sensitive information could be disrupted or exposed, so spotting warning signs early can help limit damage and restore operations. The sponsored article promotes Acronis products as a way to prevent, detect, contain, and recover from this kind of activity.

Summary
Ransomware defenders should detect and contain early behaviors such as defense tampering, lateral movement, data exfiltration, recovery sabotage, and mass file changes rather than waiting for encryption. This sponsored Acronis article promotes its integrated prevention, EDR/XDR, and backup capabilities for responding to those signals.

Ransomware encryption is often a late-stage action, while some data-extortion attacks steal information and threaten to leak it without encrypting files. The article says recent attacks against on-premises Microsoft SharePoint servers showed operators exploiting internet-facing systems, using stolen credentials, and legitimate administration tools to move through victim environments before deploying ransomware. It argues that defenders need to identify activity that occurs before widespread encryption, rather than relying only on changed file extensions.

The article identifies five early warning signals: attempts to disable defenses, unexpected privileged access or remote activity, unusual outbound data transfers, deletion of recovery options, and rapid file read-write-rename behavior. It recommends isolating affected systems, stopping malicious processes, preserving evidence, disabling compromised access, closing the entry point, and restoring from a known-good recovery point after detection. Sponsored by Acronis, the article promotes Acronis Cyber Platform capabilities for prevention, detection, response, and backup recovery, while noting that capabilities vary by licensing, configuration, edition, and deployment model.

  • A ransomware incident may never include file encryption, because data-extortion operators can steal information and rely solely on threats to publish it.
  • Backups can restore affected systems and data, but they cannot reverse the consequences of stolen data in double-extortion attacks.
  • Organizations should pre-authorize and test automated containment actions for clearly defined high-severity conditions before an incident occurs.
  • Attackers may use stolen credentials and legitimate administration tools to move through an environment, making suspicious behavior after access especially important to detect.
Key Points
  • 01Ransomware encryption is often a late-stage action, and some data-extortion attacks steal data and threaten to leak it without encrypting files.
  • 02The article identifies defense tampering, privilege escalation and lateral movement, data exfiltration, recovery sabotage, and pre-encryption file behavior as five high-value warning signals.
  • 03Common initial-access paths include exploiting vulnerable internet-facing systems, using stolen credentials, and social engineering.
  • 04After detecting ransomware, organizations should isolate affected workloads, stop malicious processes, preserve evidence, disable compromised access, close the exploited entry point, and restore from a known-good recovery point.
  • 05The sponsored article says Acronis Cyber Platform integrates prevention, detection, response, backup, and recovery capabilities, though availability varies by edition, configuration, deployment model, and licensing.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a sponsored, evergreen best-practice article about detecting ransomware activity before encryption, not reporting a new incident, vulnerability, or threat campaign. Its practical warning signs may be useful for general awareness, but it has low urgency and limited novelty for security professionals.

DKIM is an email signing method that helps verify that a message was authorized by a domain and was not changed after signing.
DLL concept

DMARC is an email policy check that uses SPF or DKIM alignment to help determine whether a message claiming to come from a domain should be trusted.
